4
A cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) is used to display a sound wave of frequency 2000 Hz.
The display of the CRO is shown.
1 cm
1 cm
What is the time-base setting on the CRO?
A
125 s cm–1
B
250 s cm–1
C
500 s cm–1
D
1000 s cm–1

hints: Notice the sound frequency is $2000 \, \text{Hz}$, so first work out the period $T = 1/f$ in $\mu\text{s}$.
Count how many $1 \, \text{cm}$ squares one complete sine wave occupies horizontally on the CRO screen.
Connect them with time-base $= T$ divided by the horizontal length of one cycle in $\text{cm}$.
walkthrough: Find the period of the sound wave from $T = 1/f$. With $f = 2000 \, \text{Hz}$, $T = 1/2000 = 0.0005 \, \text{s} = 500 \, \mu\text{s}$.
Use the $1 \, \text{cm}$ scale to measure the horizontal length of one cycle. Each grid square is $1 \, \text{cm}$ wide.
Count the squares: the screen shows two complete waves in $8 \, \text{cm}$, so one full wavelength occupies $4 \, \text{cm}$.
The time-base is time per cm, so divide the time for one cycle by its length: time-base $= 500 \, \mu\text{s} / 4 \, \text{cm}$.
Calculate $500/4 = 125$, giving $125 \, \mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$. This is option A.

A.explanation: One period is $500 \, \mu\text{s}$ spread over $4 \, \text{cm}$, giving $500/4 = 125 \, \mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: This is twice the correct value and results from using $2 \, \text{cm}$ for one period instead of $4 \, \text{cm}$.

C.explanation: This equals one full period per cm, so it ignores that one wave occupies $4 \, \text{cm}$ horizontally.

D.explanation: This is far too large and would give a period of $4000 \, \mu\text{s}$, corresponding to $250 \, \text{Hz}$ not $2000 \, \text{Hz}$.
